findings.summary: tc bridge sends the Master credential to /api/control/mine as well, and the test that claims otherwise never runs in the Master's real environment
findings.recommendation: Scope: instance. bin/tc puts `x-tangleclaw-bridge-credential` into the shared `headers` object when the verb is `bridge`; the aux request path (`requestJson` with `opts.aux`) copies every header except the verb, and after every non-`control` verb bin/tc fetches `/api/control/mine` as an aux request whenever `TANGLECLAW_LAUNCH_ID` is set. The Master pane always has that variable (lib/master.js mints it into `ambientEnv`), so every `tc bridge ...` the Master runs also presents the credential to a route it does not authorise. That contradicts the comment in bin/tc ("no unrelated request ever carries it"), docs/operator-bridge.md and the CHANGELOG. test/api-bridge.test.js `tc sends the credential on the bridge verb and on no other` cannot see it: its `tc()` helper sets no `TANGLECLAW_LAUNCH_ID`, so the banner fetch never happens, and its `otherCalls` come only from `whoami` and `ports`. Fix: attach the credential per request rather than per invocation (drop it in the aux branch, or add it only for paths under `/api/bridge/`), and give the spy test a `TANGLECLAW_LAUNCH_ID` so it asserts that `/api/control/mine` arrives without the header during `tc bridge status`.

findings.summary: Closing a route whose id is longer than 64 characters answers 500 and leaves no audit row
findings.recommendation: Scope: instance. `closeRoute` in lib/bridge-api.js validates `requestId` and `expectedVersion` but passes `request.params.routeId` through unchecked. For an unknown route `applyRouteWrite` records a `route-not-found` audit row carrying that id, and `bridge_audit.route_id` has `CHECK (route_id IS NULL OR length(route_id) <= 64)`. An id over 64 characters fails the check, the transaction rolls back, and server.js answers `500 INTERNAL_ERROR`: the Master sees an internal error where `404 ROUTE_NOT_FOUND` was promised, and the refusal is not audited, against the stated guarantee that every write is audited whether applied or refused. Validate the route id's shape (1 to 64 characters) in bridge-api.js before `applyRouteWrite` and answer 404 or 400, and add an API test for it. No test covers this path today.

findings.summary: applyRouteWrite's `change` contract says the callback must not write, and its only caller writes inside it
findings.recommendation: Scope: class. lib/bridge-store.js#applyRouteWrite documents `change` as returning `{refuse}` or `{set}` and states it "must not write anything itself", yet it hands the callback the `db` handle, and lib/bridge-api.js#closeRoute's callback calls `bridgeStore.routes.clearBodies(routeId, { at })` before returning its `set`. It broke because the primitive models only column updates on bridge_routes while a real transition also has side effects on sibling tables. Today the write is safe only by accident of ordering (it runs inside the transaction, after the version check, and close never refuses after clearing). The gateway state machine that follows will add every remaining transition on this primitive, so each author either copies the example (side effects in a callback the contract forbids, with nothing preventing a write followed by `{refuse}`, which commits the side effect alongside a refusal audit row) or obeys the comment and puts the side effect outside the transaction. Give the primitive one owner for side effects: let a decision return them declaratively (for example `effects: [(db) => ...]` or a named `clearBodies: true`) and have applyRouteWrite run them only on the applied path after the UPDATE succeeds; then either stop passing `db` to `change` or delete the "must not write" sentence. Members to search: every `change:` passed to applyRouteWrite (one today; expect more outside this diff as the gateway lands).

findings.summary: cross-component-contract: considerArrival reads medusa_exchanges.in_reply_to as a Hub id, but the producer stores an exchange id, so no real reply can ever be held
findings.recommendation: Scope: instance. Why it broke: the consumer was written against a hand-built fixture row rather than the producer. lib/medusa-exchanges.js#createSendIntent takes the replier's `inReplyTo` (a Hub id), looks up the answered exchange, and stores `in_reply_to: replyTarget.exchange_id` (an `mx_...` exchange id; the same file later resolves it with `store.medusaExchanges.get(row.in_reply_to)`). lib/bridge-gateway.js#considerArrival then does `bridgeStore.proofs.byHubId(sent.in_reply_to)` and `latest.hubId !== sent.in_reply_to`, both of which compare that exchange id against Hub ids. With the real sender path every genuine reply is dropped as `answers-nothing-the-bridge-sent` and then marked handled (ACKed to the Hub, so it is gone); the route stays `routed` until the pending notice. The tests pass only because `sessionReplies` in test/bridge-gateway.test.js and test/api-bridge-gateway.test.js inserts the sender row with `in_reply_to: <hub id>`, while the sendTracked stub in the same files returns `exchange.exchangeId: mx_<id>` - the fixture synthesizes a signal the producer never emits. Fix the consumer to correlate on what is actually stored: match `sent.in_reply_to` against the to-target proof's `exchangeId` (already recorded by dispatch), or resolve `store.medusaExchanges.get(sent.in_reply_to).hub_id` and compare that; the 'superseded message' check needs the same treatment. Then make the fixtures produce the reply row through `medusa-exchanges#createSendIntent`/`bindHubId` (or at minimum set `in_reply_to` to the exchange id) so the test exercises the real shape, and add one test that drives a reply through the real `medusa-send#sendTracked` with only the Hub stubbed.

findings.summary: A second dispatch of the same route version is turned into a false delivery failure and orphans the message that was actually sent
findings.recommendation: Scope: class (every caller of `advance` for a route in `accepted` with a destination: acceptInbound, routeTo, the 15-second tick, and the post-restart tick). Why it broke: dispatch relies on the send's request id (`bridge:<route>:v<version>`) for idempotency, but medusa-exchanges#createSendIntent answers a reused request id with 409 SEND_ALREADY_ATTEMPTED, and dispatch treats any non-200 as `send-unconfirmed`. Two reachable cases: (a) the tick lists the route while acceptInbound/routeTo is still awaiting `sendTracked`; the tick's dispatch gets 409, `_returnToMaster` bumps the version and queues a 'could not be confirmed as sent' failure notice, then the first dispatch's `_step('dispatch')` hits a version conflict, so no to-target proof is recorded although the message reached the session; (b) the server stops between a successful send and the `dispatch` write, and the next boot's tick does the same. findings.summary: A dispatch in flight has no state, so a second advance() turns a successful send into a failure and loses its proof
findings.recommendation: Scope: class. Why it broke: the route lifecycle has one source of truth (bridge_routes.state + version CAS in applyRouteWrite), but 'send in flight' is held only in a suspended promise, so two callers both see `accepted` with a destination. Conditions observed in lib/bridge-gateway.js: (1) dispatch() awaits medusaSend.sendTracked() between reading the route and its _step('dispatch'); (2) advance() is entered from three places with no serialisation: acceptInbound, bridge-api routeTo, and tick() every 15 s for every `accepted` route (server.js setInterval also has no re-entrancy guard, so a slow tick overlaps the next); (3) both callers derive the same Medusa requestId `bridge:<route>:v<version>`; (4) lib/medusa-exchanges.js createSendIntent refuses a reused requestId with 409 SEND_ALREADY_ATTEMPTED, and lib/medusa.js runs beforeHub synchronously before the Hub fetch, so the second caller is refused while the first is still awaiting the Hub; (5) dispatch() reads any non-200 as `send-unconfirmed` and calls _returnToMaster, whose _step('target-failed') commits at version N, clears the destination and queues a failure notice; (6) the first send then returns 200 and its _step('dispatch') gets version-conflict, so no to-target proof is recorded. Result: the message is on the Hub, the route says awaiting-master, the operator is told it could not be confirmed as sent, the target's reply is dropped as 'answers-nothing-the-bridge-sent', and a Master reroute delivers a second copy under the new version's requestId. The same refusal is what a restart between the send and its step meets, so advance()'s JSDoc ('safe to call at any time and after a restart; every step is applied once') and the test 'carries on after a restart from wherever a route stopped' do not cover a route stopped after the send intent was recorded; a Master `pin` during the await has the same effect because pin bumps the version with an empty `set`. Close it by construction rather than per site: claim the dispatch with a versioned step before the send (a `dispatching` state or equivalent column, written through applyRouteWrite), key the Medusa requestId on that claim, and have any later pass over a claimed route recover the exchange by request id (store.medusaExchanges.getByRequestId) and record the proof instead of resending or failing; treat SEND_ALREADY_ATTEMPTED as 'look up the exchange', never as a delivery failure. Search for other members: every `await` between a route read and its _step (dispatch, _summonMaster via _wakeMaster), and give tick() a single-flight guard. Add a test that runs two advance() calls on one accepted route with the send stub held open.

findings.summary: Once-only marks and the delivery ack are written outside the versioned route write, so they can disagree with the route
findings.recommendation: Scope: class. Why it broke: applyRouteWrite makes a transition and its effects atomic, but four facts about a route are kept beside it by separate statements. Conditions observed: (a) _wakeMaster stamps master_wake_at before awaiting sendSystemMessage and only logs a failure; tick() retries a route whose destination is the Master only while masterWakeAt is null, so one failed Hub call means that route's wake is never sent again. (b) master_wake_at is once per route, not per condition: a route the Master was woken for, then routed to a project, that later fails (tick -> _returnToMaster) goes back to awaiting-master with the operator told it 'is waiting for the Project Master to route it', and _wakeMaster returns without sending. I found no record in ADR 0023 or docs/operator-bridge.md that defers Master wake to a later phase, so the builder's Phase 5 scoping is not honoured as a ruling here. (c) pending_notice_at and the unique index idx_bridge_outbound_status both encode 'this route had its status notice'; _status sets the mark, then inserts in a second statement, so a stop between them leaves a route that can never get its notice. Nothing else reads pending_notice_at. (d) _state.replyNotified is in-memory, a fourth once-only signal with different restart behaviour. (e) acknowledgeOutbound marks the outbound item delivered in one transaction and closes the route in a second; a replayed ack returns `already-delivered` and skips the close, so a stop between them leaves the route `released` with its bodies held, and since audit.compact never passes an open route, that one route blocks audit compaction for good. Consequence: an operator message waits on a Master that was never told, or a delivered answer's text is retained past confirmed delivery. Remedy by construction: make the wake and status notices effects of applyRouteWrite keyed to the route version or failure they announce (or stamp the mark only after the send succeeds), drop pending_notice_at in favour of the index, perform markDelivered and the close in one transaction, and have tick() reconcile `released` routes whose reply item is already delivered.

findings.summary: cross-component-contract: a send adopted from the Hub's answer is recorded `routed`, but the Medusa layer can never accept its reply and nobody is told
findings.recommendation: Scope: instance. dispatch() now records a route as `routed` from `answeredHubId` when bindHubId failed, but the exchange row still has no hub_id and nothing binds it later (medusa-send.js:91 is the only caller of bindHubId). Three consumers key on that missing id: (1) createSendIntent resolves a reply through `getByHubId(inReplyTo, 'send')` (medusa-exchanges.js:437), so the target's reply is refused 404 REPLY_TARGET_UNKNOWN and can never be held; (2) tick()'s routed loop looks the exchange up by `getByHubId(sent.hubId, 'send')`, gets null, and so never sees `recipient_retired` or `undeliverable` on it; (3) `_needsMaster` is false for a `routed` project route, so the Master is never told. The route waits in `routed` for a reply that cannot arrive, and the operator gets only the five-minute still-waiting notice. The sibling case (same bind failure, server stops before the dispatch step) ends `send-unconfirmed` with the Master told, so the in-process case ends in the worse place. The adoption test asserts one send and `routed`; it never sends a reply. Fix so the route cannot rest in `routed` on an exchange with no hub_id: for example retry the bind inside dispatch before recording and, if the row still has no hub_id, leave the route `accepted` and mark it unconfirmed (no resend either way, and the Master is told). Add a case that replies after an adopted send. docs/operator-bridge.md's table row and the CHANGELOG sentence ('the route proceeds') follow whichever behavior is chosen.

observations.summary: An unconfirmed send becomes routable again when its recipient workspace retires
observations.recommendation: Scope: instance. markRecipientRetired ends every open tracked exchange for a retired workspace, including one in `send_unknown` or `send_pending` with no hub_id. On the next pass dispatch() finds that exchange in FAILED_EXCHANGE_STATES and calls _returnToMaster, the request id moves on, and a Master `route` makes a second send. Retirement proves the message will not be delivered from now on; it does not prove an unknown-outcome send was not delivered before the session ended. The second copy cannot reach the retired session, it needs the Master's explicit routing, and a confirmed-delivered route is rerouted on retirement in the same way by design, so this is not rated a finding. It does contradict the sentence in docs/operator-bridge.md that an unconfirmed send is never sent again by the Master routing it, and the constant's comment that these states prove the message did not arrive. This is the one path found by which _returnToMaster is reached for an unknown outcome; whether it is acceptable is the Architect's call.
